title: How Useful Is the Theory of Disruptive Innovation?
author: Andrew A. King · Baljir Baatartogtokh

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The supplied excerpts concern disruption theory, customer dependence, institutional priorities and legacy costs in other industries. They do not address legal AI’s jagged capabilities, selective task deployment, human verification or legal operating-model redesign, so the source’s position on the cluster proposition cannot be determined.

st.t: Disruption theory: Historical examples weakly fit predictions
st.an: The source directly supports the synthesis by finding that disruption theory has rarely been tested and that only 9% of Christensen’s cited cases reportedly satisfied all four defining elements. It nevertheless recommends selective use of the theory rather than wholesale rejection, consistent with the cluster’s context-sensitive conclusion.
qs: Our first discovery was that, despite the theory’s widespread use and appeal, its essential validity and generalizability have been seldom tested in the academic literature.
They found that only nine percent of Christensen’s 77 cases actually matched all the elements of Christensen’s own theory.

kp.k: Disruption theory identifies a dilemma within good management
kp.d: The introduction reports Christensen’s explanation for incumbent failure: listening to customers, investing in the business and building distinctive capabilities can lead well-managed companies to overlook disruptive rivals. Reference 21 clarifies that the distinctive mechanism is displacement despite possessing capabilities needed to succeed, rather than failure because capabilities have become obsolete. These are claims of the theory being examined, not the authors’ empirical conclusions.
qs: Good managers face a dilemma, he argued, because by doing the very things they need to do to succeed — listen to customers, invest in the business, and build distinctive capabilities — they run the risk of ignoring rivals with “disruptive” innovations.
Christensen broke from this tradition by arguing that companies are displaced despite possessing the capabilities needed to succeed.

kp.d: King and Baatartogtokh argue that disruption theory’s essential validity and generalizability had seldom been tested despite its popularity. They report its extension beyond business to poverty, health care access, illiteracy and unemployment, alongside Christensen’s own concern that people stretch the concept to justify predetermined intentions. The introduction poses predictive power as a question to investigate, rather than establishing it.
qs: Our first discovery was that, despite the theory’s widespread use and appeal, its essential validity and generalizability have been seldom tested in the academic literature.
Christensen and his associates have proposed disruption as a framework for thinking about vexing social problems such as poverty, lack of access to health care, illiteracy, and unemployment.
The theory, or variations thereof, has been used in so many settings that Christensen himself has expressed unease with some of the ways the theory is being applied.

kp.k: Four elements operationalize the theory’s claimed mechanism
kp.d: The reproduced UMD account describes four features tested: incumbents sustained innovation for their target market, innovation overshot customer needs, incumbents could respond to newcomers, and incumbents subsequently floundered. The captured survey separately probes whether legal or contractual barriers prevented adoption, making the capability assessment conditional on barriers as well as the ability to produce a simpler, lower-cost, profitable offering for noncustomers.
qs: Those four qualities were: Incumbents were successful at sustaining innovation in their own target market; that innovation "overshot" the needs of a substantial number of customers; the incumbents had the capability of responding to the challenge from a newcomer; and the incumbents floundered afterward.
Did legal or contractual barriers prevent these incumbent companies from developing or adopting [NAME OF DISRUPTIVE INNOVATION]?
If experts answered “yes” to A4 and there were no legal barriers (B1), then we judged that incumbents had the capability to respond.

kp.k: Expert coding favored confirmation when assessments differed
kp.d: The survey retrospectively asked experts about industry conditions before an innovation and incumbent responses afterward. Coding treated a positive answer to either the significant-market-share question or the improving-performance question as establishing leading companies with sustaining innovation trajectories. Interviewers explained that floundering could mean significant market-share loss. When experts disagreed, the relevant theoretical element was coded as confirmed.
qs: If any expert on a case responded to A1 or A2 “yes,” then we concluded leading companies with a trajectory of sustaining innovations existed.
Note: In phone interviews, we explained that “floundered” could be interpreted as having lost significant market share.

If multiple experts on the same case disagreed on the answer to a question, we gave the benefit of the doubt to the theory of disruption, and agreement with that element of the theory of disruption was judged confirmed.

kp.k: Only 9% of examples matched all four elements
kp.d: The reproduced Dartmouth Tuck write-up reports that King and Baatartogtokh surveyed 79 experts on 77 examples claimed by Christensen and found that only nine percent matched all four theoretical elements. The UMD write-up also reports 9 percent of 77 case studies. These are reported findings about the fit of selected historical examples to the theory; the numerical results reach this document through institutional accounts because the article’s results section is absent.
qs: The results section of the MIT SMR article is behind the publisher's paywall and is not held.
In it, King and co-author Baljir Baartartogtokh surveyed 79 experts on 77 examples of disruption claimed by Christensen.
They found that only nine percent of Christensen’s 77 cases actually matched all the elements of Christensen’s own theory.

kp.k: Incumbent survival complicates the displacement narrative
kp.d: The reproduced UMD account reports that incumbents survived or thrived in 39 percent of cases described as disruption. This is an institutional restatement of the study’s historical findings, not a forecast of incumbent outcomes in other markets.
qs: Fully 39 percent of the time, for instance, incumbents survived or even thrived after being disrupted, King and Baatartogtokh found.

kp.k: Use disruption alongside other strategic perspectives
kp.d: As quoted in the Dartmouth Tuck account, the authors reject both a single explanatory viewpoint and a single prescription for the challenges in their sample. They recommend retaining the best parts of disruption theory alongside classical strategic analysis rather than discarding it. This is a cross-domain management recommendation, not a claim about AI or legal-services restructuring.
qs: The threats faced by the companies in our sample were deeply challenging, and they cannot be understood from a single viewpoint or solved by a single prescription

Instead, managers need to evaluate difficult problems from a number of different perspectives. In that spirit, we do not advocate discarding the theory of disruption. Rather, we recommend using its best parts in addition to classical approaches to strategic analysis.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: King and Baatartogtokh claim that disruptive innovation theory fits relatively few of its own cited examples and should be used alongside other strategic perspectives rather than as a single explanation or prescription.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain source about business competition, not a source making claims about AI or legal services. The open introduction says the theory's validity and generalizability have seldom been tested. Institutional summaries attribute to King and Baatartogtokh the findings that only 9% of 77 purported disruption cases exhibited all four defining features, and that incumbents survived or thrived in 39% of cases. The authors recommend retaining the theory's best parts while supplementing them with classical strategic analysis. Christensen's explanation of incumbent failure is the theory being examined, not a prediction endorsed by King and Baatartogtokh.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence is a retrospective expert assessment of 77 examples attributed to Christensen, with 79 experts reported in the Dartmouth Tuck summary.
pts.d: The supplied record does not contain the article's results section; the headline findings are available through the reproduced Dartmouth Tuck and UMD institutional accounts, not independent replications. The included survey method asks about established incumbents, performance improvement, customer-needs overshoot, capability to produce a simpler and cheaper profitable offering, legal or contractual barriers, and subsequent incumbent floundering. Coding favored confirmation of the theory when experts disagreed. These are historical case assessments rather than prospective forecasting tests or AI benchmarks.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings concern historical cases examined for a 2015 publication, not a dated forecast of future disruption.
pts.d: The references list expert interviews from 2014–2015. Survey questions distinguish conditions before the innovation's arrival from incumbents' responses afterward, using case-specific base years rather than a common observation period. The four-feature fit requires sustaining innovation, overshooting customer needs, capability to respond, and subsequent floundering. The authors qualify their strategic recommendation by emphasizing multiple perspectives; they do not claim the theory is wholly worthless or specify when future incumbents will fail.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The source concerns incumbent businesses facing innovative competitors and managers deciding how to respond.
pts.d: The cases span industries rather than a specific legal market. Incumbent outcomes include significant market-share loss, survival, and thriving; managers are advised to evaluate threats through more than one strategic framework. Customers and non-customers enter the assessment through questions about oversupplied performance and simpler, lower-cost products. References to online law schools do not establish a claim about AI, law-firm displacement, or legal-service delivery in the available text.
